data.title: Štefan Janšák: Impregnable Hillforts – an essay from 1934
data.excerpt: An essay by Štefan Janšák, one of the founders of modern Slovak archaeology, on the hunt for hillforts in the field, written with self-mockery about soaked clothes, village storms and the favour of the hillfort deities. It appeared in his book Lovci hlinených perál (Hunters of Clay Beads) in 1934, in a print run of 400 copies with illustrations by Mikuláš Galanda.

children.text: We bring you an essay by one of the founders of modern Slovak archaeology, Štefan Janšák, which appeared in the book Lovci hlinených perál (Hunters of Clay Beads) in 1934. The book was published in a print run of 400 copies. The illustrations for the book were made by Mikuláš Galanda.

blocks.text: We are as superstitious as the farmers and shepherds, who see upon how many chances the success of their labour depends, and as the commanders and warriors whose all but accomplished success is spoilt by a chance wind, rain or a harsh sun. We are not ashamed of our superstition. Why, even Napoleon had his palm read, and the foremost statesmen of Rome judged the outcome of their undertakings by the colouring of the entrails of sacrificial animals. They suffered from superstition because they had to protect themselves before the public in the event of failure. And we suffer from it so that failure in the search for hillforts should not deter us.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

blocks.text: Although at home we have studied all the maps and the scholarly literature and taken counsel with this man and that, we still come with a palpable beating of the heart to the place where we are to discover a new hillfort or settlement. We walk on tiptoe, as towards a nest of little fledglings; we hold our breath, we part the bushes with care, as though a volley were awaiting us full in the breast, or as though we did not wish to disturb the idyll of lovers long estranged and only now reconciled. We half close our eyes when the decisive moment comes, like a card player, so that our disillusionment should not be too painful and, in the event of success, our agitation might be tempered. We believe in lucky and unlucky hours, and so when noon comes we do not set foot on the settlement we are seeking, but sit down to dinner a mere forty or fifty paces from the place where in a moment a „little destiny “ is to be decided. We eat our „field“ dinner with relish and throw the crumbs into the wind for the envious Poludnica, the Lady of Noon. In short, we wish to secure the co-operation of our own mood and of all the elements within us and outside us, so that at the given moment we may gather ourselves for the final step, the one crowned with a result. We are humbler, more yielding and more democratic than usual. We take our seats only in the third class of the train, we strike up friendly conversation with our neighbours, we greet the autochthonous countryfolk respectfully, and with every step we make plain how weak we are and how much we need the favour of the hillfort deities and their darlings.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

blocks.text: But sometimes the deities are hard and obstinate. Only with the greatest effort will they allow the secret they have hidden for millennia to be wrested from them. The Bošáca valley confirmed this experience for us as well. An eye as keen as Holuby's examined it for years and yet did not find the hillfort that lies right at the entrance to it, forming its very key. We took up this task after a stormy night which had driven floods of water upon the earth, refreshed the vegetation and brought with it a clear-blue, still but sultry Sunday morning. The flat hill „Turecká'' rises directly above the highway beyond Nové Mesto and seems to conceal in its name the secret of bygone ages, bound up with the miseries of the Turkish occupation and of the plundering raids upon Slovakia.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

blocks.text: We are on our first spring excursion and so we spare neither lungs, breath nor legs. We stride towards the steepest hill, to all appearances lightly and without effort. Only when trickles of sweat flood our eyes and glue our clothes to our bodies do we come to our senses and put a little prudence into our outing. But it is already too late. Excessive zeal has drenched us in a sweat that has had no time to dry even in the spring sun. The low bushes, full of dew, saw to that, emptying their still undried waterfalls down our breasts at every step. Their roguery is abetted by waist-high grass and by the forest undergrowth of broad-leaved plants, every one of which has poured out its hidden stores upon us, soaking clothing and footwear to the skin. Such a bath in warm air and beautiful sunshine is not unpleasant even when it turns out that „Turecká“ conceals nothing beneath its mysterious name. But at least we are standing on an eminence which allows us to perform the task of the cockerel in the fairy tale who flew up into a tree. Barely two kilometres away, yet separated from us by a system of deep and densely overgrown gullies, a genuinely new hill beckons to us. Perhaps that will be the longed-for ideal! Without hesitation, almost without reflection, we set off in a straight line.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

blocks.text: However much mud sticks to us on the sodden road and the ploughland, just as much is washed off by the wet grass and the forest undergrowth. However many salty drops of sweat we have to swallow as we leap over obstacles, just as many drops of insipid-tasting dew fallen from the saplings restore the balance in our mouths. Heat floods us when we walk with the wind and in the sun; cold embraces us when a sharp wind blows across the open ground. Don Cervantes could have added many a curious trait to his characters had he seen us. Here is the knight and here are the squires, and in the distance looms spot height 248, upon which an assault is being mounted.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

blocks.text: At last we are there. But just as a roguish mistress springs away from the first opening of impatient arms so that the embrace may be the sweeter, leaving the lover swooning with desire in his disenchantment, so we too stand full of astonishment with our mouths open. The small fort which must be here, as the single sherd we found indicated to us, lies a further two hundred paces off. But this time it has not escaped us! The plentiful booty made up for the effort expended so far and gave us an appetite for new investigations. We are on the small fort. It ceases to be a mystery to us. And once we have inspected it inquisitively, even unceremoniously, from every side, it almost ceases to interest us. Such is man! Hastily we gather the necessary geographical, topographical, geological and archaeological evidence and run on, after new horizons.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

blocks.text: Perhaps that is why the hillfort gods punished us, seeing human ingratitude. In Trenčín we eat our late dinner in haste, amid rain and thunder such as only diluvial upheavals could boast of. But we do not lose hope of a quick change in the weather, as is the rule with storms. One more task awaits us: to find the key to the second valley, in which Drietoma lies. „Hradištje Berg “, as our Viennese guide announces to us (the special map of the Military Geographical Institute in Vienna), stands directly above the village of Kostolná. There will be mud and dew, to be sure, but those are the least of the obstacles that stand in our way.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

blocks.text: We had indeed left the Trenčín rain belt, but the first drops were already beating on our heads as we began, to the great astonishment and consternation of the villagers, to climb the hill. The council of citizens hastily assembled in front of the tavern could not agree on the instructions we needed to find our bearings. At length an old Gypsy stepped forward resolutely, citing as his testimonials his years of service in the army, his local origin and half a dozen well-brought-up children, and offered himself as our escort. We accepted willingly, although the rain was strengthening and thickening. Don Quixote set out boldly, the pair of Sancho Panzas with a vague shrug of the shoulders, and the Gypsy in the hope of some gain. We are almost halfway up the hill when the thunder begins to roll and the rain to pour with such force that within five minutes we are soaked to the skin again. Are we to go under a tree or not? To turn back or to stay? Pride and obstinacy take hold of us. The need to preserve decorum in the face of the gods' disfavour and the fear of the villagers' mockery rise before our eyes. On top of that we are burdened by the unfortunate knowledge from physics that thunder strikes trees. The Gypsy, soaked through, consoles and encourages us, recalling all the great storms that he and his whole kin had ever lived through. But nothing helped us. Nature triumphed. It set thunder and lightning between us and the hillfort.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

blocks.text: A long May day, only half past four in the afternoon, and we must turn back without a result! And in what a state, at that! Every waterproof coat has given up the service. We are thoroughly wet, today perhaps for the fifth time and this time definitively and irrevocably, for the sun has vanished behind the clouds. Our wretched outward appearance is matched perhaps only by our inner dejection, brought on by the failure. Away from this place, where the mocking faces of the villagers grin at us from behind the windows! They are used to a soaking, to be sure, but not on a Sunday, in their holiday clothes, and not for such folly as the search for clay beads. Away from here, where the hillfort deities were not satisfied with pouring floods of water down our collars, but send it to us once again down the hillside in gurgling streams that reach to our calves! Over this sad, indeed tragicomic scene the curtains of the motor car are drawn — a car which was shortly turned into an improvised drying room, having first sprinkled the broad road at length with the water draining from us in abundance. We avoided, of course, every encounter with inquisitive eyes, lest our wholly peculiar travelling attire should bring about some enforced stop at a gendarmerie or police station.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

blocks.text: From this mishap, however, we carried away the insight that even the hillfort deities who sent the storm down upon us have a sense of class and social stratification, and evidently belong themselves among the ten thousand of the elect. For only one of the Sancho Panzas brought a head cold back from the expedition, whereas the leader and knight came away unharmed. Certainly a remarkable archaeological insight as well.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák
